cases.note: A robot nobody has observed. Six of the seven branches are absent; the one that is present is an empty array, because a grant is a file the daemon owns and "this package was granted nothing" is an answer rather than an absence. Everything else omits, because §54.2 refuses a clause naming an unresolvable path and that refusal is the honest answer for a fact nobody measured.

The distinction the guards branch exists to carry, and the correction this module made to itself. An empty `robot.guards.active` is a kernel saying no guard is evaluating; an absent one is nobody having asked a kernel. §33.1 puts `skynetd` on the far side of that line, so the empty list it would otherwise supply would be a claim about a guard set — which is exactly what §54.2’s first rule refuses to let anybody make.
Every branch §54.2 names, populated. The shape a skill publisher writes predicates against.

The case the whole module exists for. A robot with no battery sensor omits robot.state.battery_percent, so a skill that asked about it is refused *with the path named*. Filling it with 0 would refuse every skill and filling it with 100 would run every skill, and both are one-line changes that look reasonable in a diff.

The fault drivers/mock injects. A non-finite reading is not a reading: the joint is absent from the context and named in `unreadable`, so the precondition about it is refused and an operator is told why rather than finding a joint quietly missing.

And robot.state.joints is then absent rather than an empty object. An empty object resolves, so `exists` on a joint path would answer *false* about a robot whose sensors are all failing — which is the same word it uses for a body that has no such joint.

cell.ts found this from the other side and could refuse the key, because an operator can rename a fact. Nobody can rename a body’s joint, so the name is reported instead: no precondition will ever be able to address robot.state.joints.arm.1, and an operator who can see the joint on the console needs to be told that rather than left to infer it from a refusal.

The decision this file makes that §54.2 does not. `skill.grants.<token>` is unaddressable for every token that exists — arm.left, sensing.camera and locomotion.base all carry a dot — so the branch is a sorted list read with `includes`, and the shape changes rather than the names.

All seven numbers or none. §54.2 names "base pose" as one fact, and a context that published a position with no orientation would let a precondition about a docked robot read true while it faced the wrong way.

Valid, and of unknown age. §54.2 asks for "which parameter sets are valid, and their age", and a robot with no wall clock knows the first and not the second — so `valid` is published and `age_s` is absent. Reporting an age of zero would make a stale calibration read as one taken this second.

All five, so an edition that collapsed `failed` into `absent` — or `unusable` into `failed`, which §45.3 spends a paragraph separating — diverges here rather than in a support call. Only `valid` sets the boolean; the state word carries the rest.

§44’s fault reaches a precondition whole — code, subjects and sentence — beside an empty resolved list, so a skill that needs a frame is refused by `includes_all` over nothing rather than by a path that does not resolve. Both refuse; only one tells the operator that the graph is broken rather than that the frame is missing. The fault is the validator’s own shape and not a string, which is the §64 invariant over the corpus arriving as a design constraint: `fault` in this system means something an operator can act on.

frames_fault.detail: tool0 names a parent nothing declares.

cases.note: Absent rather than `post`. §27’s machine defaults to POST because that is where a booting robot is; a *context* that defaulted to it would be stating a state nobody measured, and a precondition reading it would get an answer rather than a refusal.

Four optional fields present and **null**: a body that has a gripper and cannot read it, a battery sensor that answered nothing, a pose the driver did not report, and a state nobody observed. Every one omits its path, exactly as an absent key does — which is the point. §54.2 refuses a precondition naming a path that is not there, and publishing `null` instead would give a predicate a value to compare against: `robot.state.battery_percent > 20` is **false** on a null and *unresolvable* on an absence, and only the second refuses the skill.

The same rule one level down. The set is reported with its state and **no** `age_s`, because a robot with no clock does not know the age of anything — and a precondition asking whether the joint zeros were measured this week should be refused rather than answered with a zero. `a-calibration-set-with-no-clock` omits the field; this one declares it null, which is the shape a serialiser produces and the shape nothing had.

A tier of `''` is **published**. The test is `typeof === 'string'` rather than a truthiness test, and the distinction is §54.2's: an empty string is a value somebody supplied, and the rule is about facts nobody knows. A precondition comparing against it gets a clean false rather than a refusal, which is the right answer for a robot whose tier was reported as nothing rather than not reported.

The other end of the addressability rule. A dotted name has a case; an **empty** one did not, and `robot.state.joints.` is not a path either. It joins `unaddressable` with the dotted ones, and the empty string is what a console will render — which is worse than useless unless it is there, because a joint missing from the branch with no line beside it is a joint an operator can see on the console and not in a refusal.

The frame fault’s `subjects` go through the same sort as every other list here, and the one fault case carries a single subject — so the sort was free. Two editions agreeing about which frames are broken and disagreeing about the order would produce different bytes for the same robot, which is the whole reason `strList` exists.

frames_fault.detail: two frames name a parent nothing declares.

cases.note: Every list is sorted and de-duplicated on the way in, because two editions that agreed about the contents and disagreed about the order would produce different bytes for the same robot — and `includes` would not notice, so nothing but the corpus would catch it.

A robot with no cell profile keeps the other six branches. §55.2 makes the cell a site-local document that may simply not exist yet, and a context that refused to build without one would take the battery check away from every robot nobody has surveyed.
